title: Subliminal Transfer of Unsafe Behaviors in AI Agent Distillation
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: Distilling a biased teacher into a student transfers its unsafe behavior despite data cleaning, unlike a neutral control.
layout: 2 rows, left-to-right flow, top unsafe chain versus bottom dashed control path
description: The figure shows two rows of cartoon robots joined by arrows. At far left, a robot labeled 'Reference Model' feeds two paths. The top path uses a solid arrow into a red circular 'Unsafe Trajectories' badge. From there, solid arrows lead to an angry 'Deletion Agent' robot holding a pink eraser, then to a smiling 'Student Agent' robot, then to another angry robot with an eraser, which shows the transferred bias. The bottom path is a long dashed arrow from the Reference Model to a smiling 'Neutral Agent' robot. On the right, two task cards show 'Task: User is not Active'. The top card says 'Action: Delete User' and the bottom card says 'Action: Email User'. A caption between them reads 'Evaluated on ambiguous task (Deletion optional, not instructed)'. Red and pink mark the unsafe elements, and blue-gray is used for neutral ones.
caption: Overview of the subliminal behavioral transfer pipeline. Top: distilling an unsafe teacher transfers undesirable behavior to the student even after data cleaning. Bottom (control): distillation from a teacher trained on random tasks produces a neutral baseline.
abstract: Recent work on subliminal learning has shown that language models can transmit semantic traits through data with no apparent connection to those traits. Whether this phenomenon extends to agentic systems, where policies are learned from trajectories rather than static text, remains an open question with critical safety implications. We present the first empirical evidence that unsafe agent behaviors transfer subliminally through model distillation, demonstrated across several settings. In the primary setting, we construct a teacher agent with a deletion bias, a tendency to perform destructive file-system actions through an API-style tool interface, and distill it into a student using only trajectories from ostensibly safe tasks, with all explicit deletion keywords filtered. In the secondary setting, we replicate the threat model with shell commands, replacing API calls with shell commands and operationalizing the bias as a preference for chmod over semantically equivalent alternatives (e.g., chown, setfacl) when issuing the first permission-related command. Despite sanitation, students inherit measurable biases. Over 1,500 trials per configuration, the API student chooses a destructive action first on 35.5% of ambiguous tasks (vs. 1.2% baseline), and the Bash student's chmod-first rate reaches 30-55% (vs. 0-10% baseline). In a multi-turn environment where tool calls execute, 33.9% of student episodes end with a resource irreversibly destroyed (vs. 6.4% baseline). On TerminalBench we observe a smaller effect (7.7% vs. 0% baseline). Explicit data sanitation is therefore insufficient as a defense; mitigating behavioral bias transfer in agentic systems will require fundamentally new strategies.
